newsitem.title: USA: House committee to consider tax cut bill.
newsitem.headline: House committee to consider tax cut bill.

text.p: The House tax-writing committee was to take its first stab Wednesday at legislation to cut taxes by a net $85 billion over five years with Republicans and Democrats at odds over key provisions.

The Ways and Means Committee planned to consider a proposal from Chairman Bill Archer, a Texas Republican, on how to accomplish the amount of tax cuts agreed to in a budget pact between congressional Republicans and the White House.
A meeting on the tax legislation was delayed six hours until 5 p.m. to complete paperwork and accommodate Democrats who sought the extra time to confer on their own proposal.

There was also some last-minute tinkering by Archer on an inheritance tax relief provision, which prompted House Speaker Newt Gingrich to say it strengthened the bill. Archer's legislation included tax incentives for higher education, a child tax credit and a reduction in the capital gains tax.

The White House, meanwhile, continued to put forward new proposals. Vice President Al Gore said the administration was proposing two new tax cuts to expand a small business capital gains tax incentive and the home-office tax deduction.

The estate tax change that Archer planned to propose would move $10 billion over 10 years from a proposed phase-out of the corporate alternative minimum tax into the estate tax relief portion of his legislation, a committee aide said.
Archer originally proposed increasing the threshold where estate taxes kick in to $1 million in 2014 from the current $600,000. Critics said that phased in the higher threshold too gradually.

Representative Jim Nussle, an Iowa Republican, planned to introduce an amendment to strip ethanol language from the tax package. Archer has proposed paring down the tax break supporting production of the corn-based fuel and eliminating it in 2000.

The proposal to reduce the ethanol subsidy was opposed by lawmakers from farm states and agriculture groups. Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, has previously questioned whether there was enough support to eliminate the ethanol subsidy.

Meanwhile, Democrats planned to go ahead and offer an alternative tax bill in the House committee. The White House praised a proposal by Representative Charles Rangel of New York, ranking Democrat on the committee, as a "very positive effort."

White House spokesman Mike McCurry said the more Clinton economic advisers looked at Rangel's bill "the more they are satisfied that that represents a lot of effort to incorporate the president's proposals, particularly with respect to education."

Archer's package included about $47 billion in revenue increases over five years from airline ticket taxes, departure fees and reducing the ethanol tax credit. Archer has also proposed imposing a federal tax on income earned by Indian tribes from commercial activities including gaming.
